method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory of two reference books; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the people and their years, the appellation decrees, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and every beat of the story.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (Wine With Seth, Wine Anorak, Burgundy Report) and the importer's site, whose address carries a living person's name, were read as leads and never cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile (hectares and present managers met in results, none carried), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. changed.was: Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) took over his family's vines at Villié-Morgon in 1973, when Beaujolais was riding the fashion for Nouveau and most of it was made with cultured yeast, added sugar and plenty of sulphur. Towards the end of that decade he came under the influence of Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), a négociant and chemist of the Beaujolais whose work on yeasts and fermentation argued that healthy grapes, carefully handled, needed nothing added. Lapierre took the lesson into his vines and his cellar: he gave up herbicides, picked late and sorted hard, put whole bunches into cooled vats, left the fermentation to the native yeasts, stopped adding sugar and used little or no sulphur. Neighbouring growers in Morgon worked the same way, and abroad the four became known as the Gang of Four, a critic's phrase rather than a society. His Morgon found drinkers far beyond the Beaujolais, and the natural wine movement took it as a model. After his death in 2010 his son and daughter carried the domaine on as he had made it. The movement's argument fits in this one bottle: nothing added, and everything decided in the vineyard.
changed.now: The Lapierre family's estate at Villié-Morgon dates, by its own account, from 1909, and Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010), born in the village, took it over from his father in 1973. In 1981, under the guidance of Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), a négociant and chemist of the Beaujolais whose research on yeasts and fermentation argued that sound grapes, carefully handled, needed little added, he changed course: he farmed organically, picked by hand and sorted hard, put whole bunches into vat, left the fermentation to the native yeasts, stopped adding sugar and used little or no sulphur. Neighbouring growers in Morgon worked the same way, and in America, where their importer gave them the name, the four became known as the Gang of Four, a nickname rather than a society. His Morgon found drinkers far beyond the Beaujolais, and the natural wine movement took it as a model. He died in October 2010, just after the harvest, and his son and daughter carried the domaine on as he had made it, bottling the Morgon in some years both with and without sulphur. The movement's argument fits in this one bottle: nothing added, and everything decided in the vineyard.
changed.why: Chauvet's guidance is 1981 by the domaine and Vinous; the Gang of Four was named by the growers' American importer (Wine Scholar Guild, Verve, and the Codex's own master bank); the estate of 1909 and the takeover from his father are the domaine's; late picking, cooled vats and the region's cellars of 1973 had no source.

changed.was: Morgon's growers have an old verb for what their wine does with age: it morgonne, taking on a kirsch and a savour that set it apart from the lighter crus. At the heart of the cru rises the Côte du Py, a hill of decomposed schist rich in iron and manganese whose wines are slow to open, and Morgon became an appellation of its own in 1936. The grower whose name the domaine carries took over his family's vines at Villié-Morgon in 1980, when much of the village sold its wine young for the Nouveau trade. Close to Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) and to the teaching of the chemist Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), he gave up herbicides, cultured yeast, added sugar and most of the sulphur, and let whole bunches ferment slowly in the cool. Abroad the four Morgon growers who worked this way became known as the Gang of Four. Foillard's Côte du Py, raised in barrels bought from Burgundy domaines, became the bottle that showed how deep and long lived Gamay made with nothing added could be. Open a ten year old bottle for the guest who says Beaujolais never ages: the hill, not the cellar, is what makes it last.

changed.was: Mont Brouilly stands on its own at the southern end of the crus, a hill of hard blue stone among the granite, and in 1857, as the story goes, the growers built a chapel on its summit to pray for protection from the oidium that was ruining their vines. Twenty years later, in 1877, an ancestor of the Geoffray family bought Château Thivin on the flank of the hill, and his given name lives on in the estate's old vine Cuvée Zaccharie. changed.now: Mont Brouilly stands on its own at the southern end of the crus, a hill of hard blue stone among the granite. Shaken by the vine plagues of the nineteenth century, the growers raised a chapel on its summit in 1857, Notre-Dame du Raisin, to ask protection from the oidium that was ruining their vines. Twenty years later, on 8 June 1877, a grower from the nearby hamlet of Durette and his wife bought Château Thivin at a public sale, with a small holding of vines on the flank of the hill, and the Geoffray family's story on the hill begins there. The family worked vines on several faces of the hill, each ripening at its own pace. The growers of the slopes formed their own association in 1934, and the decree of 19 October 1938 gave them an appellation of their own, Côte de Brouilly, apart from the larger Brouilly that rings the foot of the hill. Thivin, fermenting parcel by parcel in its hillside cellars, showed what the hill gives Gamay: a firmer frame and a saline bite. changed.was: In 1395 Philip the Bold (1342 to 1404), Duke of Burgundy, ordered Gamay torn out of the Côte d'Or as a disloyal plant, and the grape found its home further south, on the granite hills of the Beaujolais. Moulin-à-Vent takes its name from the old windmill above Romanèche-Thorins, not from any village, and when it became an appellation in 1936 its wines were already among those the region kept for years, firm from the manganese in its granite. Château des Jacques, an estate at Romanèche-Thorins with vines in several climats of the cru, was bought in 1996 by Maison Louis Jadot, the Beaune merchant house founded in 1859. The new owners treated it as they would a domaine of the Côte d'Or: they named and bottled the climats apart, Clos de Rochegrès, Clos du Grand Carquelin, Champ de Cour and others, destemmed the grapes and aged the wines in barrel. Rochegrès showed that one walled vineyard of Gamay could carry its own name and age like Burgundy, and it brought the Burgundian idea of the climat back to the grape Burgundy had once banished. Rochegrès puts Beaujolais back beside Burgundy on a list, where its grape began.
changed.now: On 31 July 1395 Philip the Bold (1342 to 1404), Duke of Burgundy, ordered Gamay torn out of the Côte d'Or as a very bad and disloyal plant, and the grape held its ground further south, on the granite hills of the Beaujolais, beyond his lands. Moulin-à-Vent takes its name from the old windmill above Romanèche-Thorins, not from any village, and it became an appellation by the decree of 11 September 1936, its vines in Romanèche-Thorins and Chénas. Château des Jacques, an estate at Romanèche-Thorins with vines in several clos of the cru, belonged to the Thorin family until 1996, when it was bought by Maison Louis Jadot, the Beaune house founded in 1859. Under Jadot the estate replanted part of its vineyard, added vines in Morgon in 2001 and renovated its winery in 2017. It destems its grapes and ages its wines in barrel, as a domaine of the Côte d'Or would, and bottles its clos apart, Clos de Rochegrès, Clos du Grand Carquelin, Champ de Cour and La Roche among them. Rochegrès, from the highest ground of the cru, shows that one clos of Gamay can carry its own name and age like Burgundy, bringing the Burgundian idea of the climat back to the grape Burgundy once banished.
changed.why: The edict's date and words are The Drinks Business's and Wine Spectator's; the decree's date and communes the INAO's; the Thorin family, the replanting, the Morgon vines of 2001 and the winery of 2017 the château's; manganese as the cause of the cru's firmness had no source.

tested: Georges Duboeuf's years (Decanter, Wein.plus and Wikipedia: born 14 April 1933, died at his home in Romanèche-Thorins on 4 January 2020, aged 86; one French outlet says 87): confirmed, 1933 to 2020.
His birth and family (Wikipedia: Crêches-sur-Saône; other accounts: Chaintré, where the family had long grown vines): the record says a family of growers in the Mâconnais.

The bicycle (Grape Collective and other accounts: at eighteen, in 1951, he delivered wine by bicycle to restaurants and chefs, Lyon among them; the house's site names chefs he visited): kept, told as a story.
The house of 1964 (Wikipedia and the library): confirmed.
The flower labels (the house, in his own words: the idea came to him in the 1970s; the house's Flowers collection carries Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie and Beaujolais-Villages): confirmed and dated.

Nouveau in 1951 and 1985 (Inter Beaujolais: the growers' union asked to sell before the release of 15 December, granted by a note of the tax authorities of 13 November 1951, first sale on 15 November; the third Thursday fixed in 1985; the INAO's Beaujolais specification agrees on the third Thursday): confirmed and the 1951 story corrected.

Nouveau abroad (the house: the new wine reached North America, Australia and Japan in the 1980s, and he went each year to open the first bottles; Taste France: the races spread abroad in the 1980s): the race to pour on one day in four named cities softened to the house's account.

The making (no sheet of the house's Nouveau found; its Beaujolais sheets: semi carbonic maceration of six to eight days, pressing, controlled temperatures, steel): vats filled with carbon dioxide corrected to the semi carbonic way.
Beaujolais-Villages Nouveau (the house's wines page lists it): confirmed; a little firmer cut.
The rules: his son, who took over in 2018, is living and is not named (in people.json); no price, no score, no volume (Japan's bottle count met in results, not carried): sound.

changed.was: The young wine of the Beaujolais was poured in the bistros of Lyon long before it had a legal name, and in 1951 the authorities allowed the region to sell its new wine before the usual date in December, which made Beaujolais Nouveau an official category. Georges Duboeuf (1933 to 2020), born to a family of growers in the Mâconnais, began by selling his family's white wine to the restaurants of Lyon, delivering it himself, as the story goes, by bicycle. In 1964 he set up his own business at Romanèche-Thorins, buying wine from growers across the region, bottling it under his own name and giving the whole range one recognisable look, with flower labels for the crus. He made Nouveau an event: bottles were trucked, shipped and flown so that the new wine could be poured on the same day in Paris, London, New York and Tokyo, and in 1985 the release was fixed on the third Thursday of November. The fashion carried the name Beaujolais round the world and left the region a reputation for simple wine that its crus have worked for decades to live down. For a sommelier the bottle is a date on the calendar and a lesson in carbonic maceration.
changed.now: In 1951 the growers' union of the Beaujolais asked to sell its new wine before the general release of 15 December, and a note of the tax authorities of 13 November that year allowed it: Beaujolais Nouveau went on sale from 15 November. Georges Duboeuf (1933 to 2020), born to a family of growers in the Mâconnais, began at eighteen, as the story goes, by delivering wine by bicycle to the restaurants and chefs of the region, Lyon among them. In 1964 he set up his own business at Romanèche-Thorins, buying wine from growers across the region and bottling it under his own name, and from the 1970s, by his own account, he dressed his crus in flower labels. He made the November release an event, and by the house's account the new wine reached North America, Australia and Japan in the 1980s, where he went each year to open the first bottles. In 1985 the release was fixed on the third Thursday of November. The fashion carried the name Beaujolais round the world. He died at his home in Romanèche-Thorins in January 2020. For a sommelier the bottle is a date on the calendar and a lesson in carbonic maceration.
changed.why: The 1951 story is Inter Beaujolais's; the bicycle at eighteen is several accounts', told as a story; the flower labels of the 1970s are his own account; the 1980s abroad are the house's; his death is Decanter's; the bistros of Lyon before 1951, the four named cities and the crus living down a reputation had no source.
